catalog_quote: In EA stress is not a major problem, as its occurrence is almost totally predictable in terms of syllable structure. As in English, a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress; and long vowels never occur unstressed. Remember that EA does not permit more than one long vowel in a word; in case of two long vowels (resulting from morphological suffixation), the first gets shortened and the stress shifts to the second long vowel ... Bearing the above in mind, we can state the rules for EA stress as follows: GENERAL RULE: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable; e.g. /katab/ 'he wrote,' ... /madrasa/ 'school.' EXCEPTIONS: (a) Stress falls on the last syllable if it has the structure CVCC or CVV(C); e.g. /katabt/ 'I wrote,' ... /ramuu/ 'they threw it' (m), /hinaak/ 'there.' (b) Stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable if the last three syllables have the structure: CVCVCV(C)…
sweep_summary: Egyptian (Cairene) Arabic is in the catalog as weight-sensitive on Abdel-Massih 1975. Of 13 title hits, 9 are about Cairene word stress, 3 are intonation/discourse prosody (Hellmuth 2006 x2, Hellmuth 2007, Ward & Al Bayyari 2007) and one is a general theory (Hagberg). Two were obtained open and read: Welden 1980 'Stress in Cairo Arabic' (SLS 10(2), whole volume on archive.org; IDEALS hdl 2142/9324) and Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Book 3, via Internet Archive copy of the SIL PDF). Welden gives a first-hand, informant-tested rule (p. 102) that confirms every clause of the catalog's rule (penult default; final CVCC/CVV(C); LLL antepenult; final CVC light; katabítu penult) and refines it (alternating count for all-light strings, unstressed long vowels shorten, proclitics outside the domain, secondary rhythmic stress exists, p. 111); it is a better deciding source than the textbook and should replace or head the citation, with the 'weight' coding unchanged. Hagberg reproduces Hayes' 1991 Cairene rule (p. 7) second-hand, consistent with both. Aquil 2014's abstract (Crossref) states primary stress is uncontroversially on one of the last three syllables and argues secondary stress exists (refines the catalog's 'no secondary stress' note). Not obtainable by automated download: McCarthy 1979 LI (JSTOR; UMass ScholarWorks 403), Welden 1977 UT Austin diss., Guindy 1988 ZAL, Harms 1981 Linguistic Analysis, Larudee 1973 Language Sciences, Hayes 1995 (Google Books preview only), Hellmuth 2006/2007 (SOAS eprints unreachable; De Gruyter paywalled).org, IDEALS, MPI PuRe and the the Internet Archive.

new_statements.quote: A CV syllable is light, as is a word-final CVC. [...] CVC when non-final is heavy. CVV, CVVC and CVCC are always heavy. [...] Statement I: Stress does not regress beyond the ante-penult. A light syllable is not stressed in final position. Statement II: The last heavy syllable is stressed in either ultimate or penultimate position, but not in ante-penultimate position. Statement III: If no heavy syllable occurs, or if it precedes the penult, stress is placed on the penultimate syllable, except in the case of words of the following shape LLL, in which the ante-penult is stressed.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, right-edge, three-syllable window: final syllable stressed only if superheavy (CVVC/CVCC) or CVV; otherwise a heavy penult (non-final CVC, CVV) is stressed; a heavy antepenult is never stressed (mádrasa); among all-light strings the count decides (LLL -> antepenult kátabu; LLLL -> penult katabítu, generalized as even -> penult, odd -> antepenult); final CVC counts light; unstressed long vowels shorten; proclitics are outside the stress domain; secondary rhythmic stress on alternate preceding syllables. This is the same system the catalog codes ('weight', CVV+CVC heavy, right edge) and matches every clause of Abdel-Massih's rule including the katabítu exception, so the classification stands.

new_statements.quote: In order to avoid the multiplication of diacritic signs, the sign for accent (') has been employed as sparingly as possible. This sign is placed at the beginning of the syllable accented; e.g. (below) ka'man (accent on second syllable), 'fahma (on first syllable). If the following two points are remembered, they will be found a sufficient guide to almost all the words which have no accent-mark: (1) a long vowel (: or ·) is invariably the accented vowel; (2) if there is no long vowel, the accent is on the last syllable but one, unless otherwise marked.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog and Welden 1980: right-edge, weight-sensitive, CVV always stressed, penult by default, long vowels shorten when unstressed, clitics shift the accent. It is a coarser pedagogical statement: it does not spell out the CVC-heavy-penult vs antepenult condition, the superheavy-ultima clause, or the even/odd light-string pattern (katabítu); those cases are handled by explicit accent marks in the text. Nothing in it contradicts the catalog. Describes the Cairo colloquial (School of Oriental Studies, Cairo; footnotes on the Alphabet page note Upper Egyptian pronunciation differences).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A practical rule for the learner: the syllable with the long (or half-long) vowel always carries the accent; if the word has no long vowel the accent falls on the penult; anything else is marked with the accent sign in the text (e.g. ka'man with final-syllable accent, the shortened reflex of kamaan). Vowel length in the notation is phonemic, so this is a weight-sensitive system in which CVV attracts the accent and the default is the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 137, footnote 1: 'Where more than one accent appears to fall on a single word-group, it will be found that the last is the strongest, and the rest secondary.' (about clitic groups such as verb + object + dative suffixes); nothing on rhythmic secondary stress inside simple words.
new_statements.exceptions: 'unless otherwise marked': words not covered by the two points carry an explicit accent sign. Suffix pronouns 'never receive accent by themselves' (p. 27) and a suffix 'throws accent on to the preceding syllable, as suffixes do' (p. 85, on dative l-+pronoun, e.g. lak); repeated notes on 'shifting of accent' with vowel elision and loss of length under suffixation and annexation (pp. 35, 45, 51, 75, 81, 129, 137); long vowels shorten when they lose the accent (p. 129: ji'bi:Su 'they sell' but jibi'Su:ha). Fuller rules are referred to the companion volume 'The Phonetics of Arabic' (pp. 68-72).
new_statements.identity_note: Both readable works describe Cairo/Lower Egyptian colloquial: Gairdner is a Cairo (School of Oriental Studies) conversation grammar whose Alphabet page footnotes note Upper Egyptian pronunciation differences; McCarthy's section is explicitly about 'a dialect spoken in Egypt from Cairo northward' and contrasts it with Damascene and with Classical Arabic as read by Cairenes.

new_statements.quote: Harrell (1957) gives three principal stress rules for this dialect, along with a few morphological exceptions: (1) a. Stress the ultima if it is a superheavy syllable (CVCC or CVVC) [...]. b. Otherwise stress the antepenultimate syllable if the antepenult and penult are light syllables (CV), unless the preantepenult is also light [...]. c. Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable [...]. [p. 105:] (4) a. Stress a superheavy ultima. b. Otherwise stress a heavy penult. c. Otherwise stress the penult or antepenult, whichever is separated by an even number of syllables from the rightmost nonfinal heavy syllable or, if there is no nonfinal heavy syllable, from the left boundary of the word.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog and as Welden 1980 (superheavy ultima, heavy penult, antepenult vs penult by parity in light strings, final CVC light). Adds: the explicit even-number parity formulation from Langendoen 1968, the metrical foot analysis, the derivation of stressed final CVV from suffixal -h, and the 3 f. sg. + clitic exception. Attributes the base rules to Harrell 1957 and the Classical-word data to Mitchell 1975. Describes the dialect 'spoken in Egypt from Cairo northward'; also treats Damascene and Classical Arabic separately.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cairene: a superheavy final syllable (CVVC, CVCC) is stressed; otherwise a heavy penult (CVC, CVV) is stressed; otherwise the penult or antepenult is stressed according to parity, counting light syllables in pairs from the left edge of the word or from the rightmost non-final heavy syllable (búxala, katabítu, ?inkásara, muxtálifa). A word-final CVC counts as light (mudárris, ?ábadan); heavy antepenults reject stress (martába, yiktíbu). Formalised as binary left-to-right feet over pairs of light syllables with a right-branching word tree (p. 106).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit statement about Cairene secondary stress in the Cairene section; the left-to-right binary feet imply rhythmic structure but McCarthy does not spell out secondary prominence for Arabic. Section 3.6 'Secondary Stress' (p. 180 ff.) concerns Tiberian Hebrew.
new_statements.exceptions: Final CVV is always stressed in colloquial words (ramáa 'he threw him', ?axúu) but is analysed as an underlying superheavy CVVh with suffixal h deleted (pp. 114-116); in Classical Arabic words read by Cairenes a final CVV is unstressed. Morphological exception: 3 f. sg. verb suffix -it plus an object clitic takes the stress (kallimítak, ramítu, expected *kallímitak, *rámitu; pp. 116-118), handled by a 'Feminine Adjunction' rule. Harrell's rule fails for long light strings in Classical words read by Cairenes (baqarátuhu, sajarátuhu, p. 105), which the parity rule (4c) covers.
new_statements.identity_note: Both readable works describe Cairo/Lower Egyptian colloquial: Gairdner is a Cairo (School of Oriental Studies) conversation grammar whose Alphabet page footnotes note Upper Egyptian pronunciation differences; McCarthy's section is explicitly about 'a dialect spoken in Egypt from Cairo northward' and contrasts it with Damascene and with Classical Arabic as read by Cairenes.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Abdel-Massih 1975 scanned at sec. 7.5, pp. 25-26 (page images also held); locator correct. (2) Deciding source is a 1975 pedagogical textbook, but the held 1979 Reference Grammar by the same authors (p. 254) states identical rules, and Woidich 1980 (Handbuch der arabischen Dialekte, pp. 210-211), downloaded now from the Rosetta Project scan, independently confirms the weight-driven right-edge rule (stress the last vCC / long-vowel sequence if at most one syllable follows, else the vowel immediately after it; initial stress when no heavy sequence exists; 3fs-perfect and certain plurals morphologically fixed). Coding classification weight, edge=right, what counts as heavy: CVV+CVC (final CVC not stress-attracting, final CVCC/CVV(C) attracting) is exactly what all three say and matches the well-known generative literature. sources.quote: (9) Stress in Cairene Arabic: a. Stress is on the last syllable, if it is superheavy. b. Otherwise, stress is on the penult, if it is heavy. c. Otherwise, stress is on the antepenult or penult, whichever is separated by an even number of syllables from the immediately preceding heavy syllable, if there is one, or from the beginning of the word if there is none, where zero is counted as even.

sources.note: General theory; uses Cairene Arabic as the type case of left-headed moraic trochees (Sect. 1.2.2 pp. 7-9, Sect. 3.1.2.1). Second-hand data (Langendoen 1968, McCarthy 1979, Halle & Vergnaud 1987) and Hayes' (1991) rule: final superheavy syllable stressed; else heavy penult; else antepenult or penult, whichever is an even number of syllables from the preceding heavy syllable (or word start). sources.quote: There is no dispute in the literature over the place of primary stress, on one of the rightmost three syllables. However, very few studies support the presence of secondary stress (Harms, 1981; Welden, 1980), while more research suggest that secondary stress does not exist (Aljarah, 2008; De Lacy, 1998; Halle & Vergnaud, 1987; Hayes, 1995; Kenstowicz, 1994; McCarthy, 1979; Watson, 2002). Although I agree with research (Gairdner, 1926; Harms, 1981; Welden, 1980) that secondary stress exists in CA, I refute the data and analysis proposed by this research.
sources.note: Abstract (Crossref): primary stress uncontroversially on one of the rightmost three syllables; argues with OT constraints (FootBinarity, Align-Head/R, Trochaic, WSP, *Clash, *Lapse) that secondary stress exists, siding with Gairdner 1926, Harms 1981, Welden 1980 against Hayes 1995, McCarthy 1979, Watson 2002 etc., while refuting the earlier data. Refines the catalog's 'no secondary stress described' field; primary-stress coding unaffected. Full text paywalled.
